newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. senator recommends U.S.-Israel-Syria summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator recommends U.S.-Israel-Syria summit.

text.p: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter said on Thursday after shuttling between Israel and Syria that U.S. President Bill Clinton should invite the leaders of both countries to the White House to talk peace.

"My sense of the situation is that the next step is up to the United States and that President Clinton should invite both Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu and President (Hafez al-) Assad to the Oval office to continue the peace process," he said.
Specter spoke at an airport news conference after briefing Netanyahu on talks with Assad in Damascus that an Israeli government official said were held at the Israeli leader's behest.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu expressed hope that a way would be found to resume the peace negotiations with Syria," Netanyahu's spokesman said in a statement.
Israel's army radio said Netanyahu had sent Assad a message asking that the sides resume peace talks immediately.
The United States, sponsor of Arab-Israeli peace talks, has mediatied between Israel and Syria to defuse tensions that have risen between the arch-foes since Netanyahu took office in June.

The two countries have held sporadic peace talks for the last five years. The negotiations have long been snagged over the Golan Heights captured by Israel in 1967. Syria demands the return of the entire Golan Heights.
Israel's previous government, ousted by Netanyahu in May elections, said it could make at least a partial withdrawal for full peace.
Netanyahu rejects the principle of trading occupied Arab land for peace and negotiations between the sides have yet to resume.

"Senator Specter told the prime minister that according to Assad, there is no escalation on the Israeli-Syrian border and that recent Syrian army movements are purely routine," Netanyahu's spokesman said.
The movement of Syrian forces in September to within striking distance of a key Israeli military outpost on the Golan Heights has heightened war jitters in the Jewish state.
